issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a childhood trauma of witnessed domestic violence, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is hard to reconcile unless there is some additional perpetration or morally injurious behavior by the patient during the trauma. In this profile there are no memory or threat items indicating the patient did something blameworthy during the event, so this item is clinically hard to explain.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected
issues.explanation: 'Being criticised or corrected' can occur in many PTSD presentations, but here it is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The threat, memory, and appraisal items center on fear/safety, grief, and self-instability rather than interpersonal criticism or humiliation. Given the specified trauma and the other items selected, this trigger appears insufficiently linked to the formulation and surrounding symptoms.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For childhood witnessed domestic violence, strong self-blame can occur, but the specific wording 'the event happened because of the way I acted' is hard to reconcile with a witness-child trauma unless there is some indication she directly intervened or was held responsible. The rest of the profile does not suggest that role, so this item is clinically questionable for this trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
issues.explanation: Avoiding open or exposed spaces implies a danger formulation centered on attack in public/exposed environments. The rest of the profile's triggers and memories are strongly interpersonal/domestic (shouting, touch, body odour, grief, visual memories of domestic violence), and the threat items emphasize checking safety/startle rather than fear of exposed outdoor space. This avoidance strategy does not fit the dominant trauma-linked threat pattern and is the least coherent item cross-node.

vignette:
# Carmen's Story

Carmen was thirty-nine years old when she walked into the detective bureau one Monday morning and realized that the life she had built was no longer sustainable. She had been a detective for twelve years, respected for her work on domestic violence cases, and she lived with her partner of five years in a quiet neighborhood outside the city. To anyone who knew her, she was composed, methodical, and reliable. What no one saw was the war happening inside her every single day, a war that had its roots in a childhood she could never quite escape.

When Carmen was seven, she watched her father beat her mother in their kitchen. She remembered fragments—a flash of his raised fist, her mother's body crumpling against the refrigerator, the sound of breaking glass—but the memory existed mostly as a series of still images, vivid and terrible, that would surface without warning. Her father's sweat, the sharp animal smell of him when he was enraged, had seared itself into her sensory world. For thirty-two years, that smell haunted her. Now, whenever she encountered it—a man's sweat during an arrest, a suspect in close quarters, even the smell of her own partner after he came home from the gym—her body reacted as though she were seven again, watching her father's fist descend. Her heart would race, her breathing would tighten, and she would feel the urgent need to escape or to do something, anything, to make the panic stop.

The shouting triggered her in much the same way. On the job, when she had to interview aggressive suspects or when voices were raised in the bullpen, Carmen's threat system would activate instantly. She had come to believe that loud voices meant violence was imminent, that she was in danger, and that she needed to be ready to protect herself. But it was not just the objective threat that frightened her; Carmen had begun to interpret her own reactions as evidence that something was fundamentally wrong with her. The fact that she startle violently at unexpected movement, that she wakes at night checking the locks and windows, that she cannot sit in a restaurant without positioning herself to see the exits—these things convinced her that she was losing her mind. She was certain that her hypervigilance, her inability to relax, her conviction that danger lurks everywhere, meant that she was going crazy. This belief fed back into her threat monitoring; each time she checked the locks or positioned herself strategically in a room, she felt the shame of her own pathology, which only intensified her sense that something is profoundly broken inside her.

The physical touch was worst of all. Her partner, Miguel, had become a source of profound distress. When he tried to hold her hand, to embrace her, to be intimate with her, Carmen would feel that same sensory flash—the memory of her father's hands, violent and unpredictable—and she would recoil. She could not bear to be touched, could not allow herself to feel the comfort or closeness that Miguel desperately wanted to give her. When he approached her, especially when she was already anxious or when the encounter was unexpected, her body would interpret his touch as a threat. This conviction that touch meant danger, combined with her fear that she was fundamentally broken, led her to pull away from him entirely. She had begun to avoid him, to stay late at work, to sleep in the spare room. She told herself that she was protecting him from her, that he deserved someone who was not damaged, someone who could love him normally.

The maladaptive strategies had emerged gradually, almost without her noticing. When the triggers—the smell of sweat, the shouting, the unexpected touch—would activate her threat response, Carmen would hurt herself to escape the cascade of memory and panic. She would dig her nails into her palms, press ice against her skin, sometimes cut herself with a razor blade she kept hidden in her desk drawer at the precinct. The physical pain was a relief, a way to interrupt the unbearable flood of images and emotion. She had also become expert at avoiding anything that might trigger a feeling—positive or negative. She stopped going to social events, stopped listening to music, stopped allowing herself to hope for anything, because hope could be disappointed, and disappointment led to vulnerability, and vulnerability meant she might remember. She avoided her partner's touch so completely that Miguel had stopped trying to comfort her. The self-harm and emotional avoidance also kept the traumatic memories at bay; when she was hurting herself or numb, the images of her mother's face and her father's fist receded into the background.

Yet these strategies came at a cost. The more Carmen avoided feeling, the more isolated she became. The more she hurt herself to cope with triggers, the more convinced she became that she was unstable, that her reactions were proof of her own weakness or worthlessness. She had come to believe that the violence she witnessed as a child had happened because of who she was—that somehow her presence, her very existence, had provoked it. When she tried to deliberately remember the event, to understand it rationally as an adult, the memory would fragment and slip away, leaving only the images and the overwhelming grief that would wash over her when they surfaced unbidden. That grief—the profound sadness and helplessness of being seven years old and unable to stop her father from hurting her mother—would trigger her self-harm again, which would then reinforce her belief that she was going crazy, which would make her more hypervigilant, which would make her startle at shadows and check the locks obsessively.

The cycle had tightened over months and years. Carmen's threat system remained chronically activated, always scanning for danger, always ready to react. Her avoidance of touch had deteriorated her relationship with Miguel to the point where he was threatening to leave. Her self-harm had left small scars on her inner wrists and thighs. And her belief that she was fundamentally broken, that her reactions were proof of her own pathology rather than a reasonable response to what she had witnessed, kept her trapped in a loop of shame and isolation. It was only when Miguel finally said, "I can't watch you disappear," that Carmen realized she needed help. She came to her first therapy session terrified that a clinician would confirm what she already knew: that she was damaged beyond repair, that the little girl who watched her father's violence had been marked by it in ways that could never be undone.
